Title: Debate y polémica en el Senado por elección de Carlos Camargo a la Corte Constitucional

Summary: 
The Colombian Senate held a marathon session of more than six hours to elect Carlos Camargo Assis, former Ombudsman, as a new magistrate of the Constitutional Court for the 2025‑2033 term.  Camargo won with 62 votes out of 103 possible, surpassing María Patricia Balanta who received 41 votes, while the third candidate, Jaime Humberto Tobar, received no support.  The election replaced José Fernando Reyes Cuartas, whose eight‑year term had ended.  The vote was marked by political tensions: the executive had backed Balanta, and the Senate was divided over the legitimacy of the electoral process.  Senator Isabel Zuleta declared herself impeded due to a potential conflict of interest, and the National Electoral Council (CNE) abruptly revoked the voting rights of Congresswoman Ana María Castañeda of Cambio Radical, a decision she contested.  Castañeda defended her right to vote, saying, 'La política se dignifica cuando se ejerce con libertad, no con sometimiento. Estoy habilitada y no voy a permitir que se vulneren mis derechos'.  Despite her protest, the plenary ratified the CNE’s decision, later allowing both Castañeda and Senator Temístocles Ortega to vote under the condition that they could be held legally accountable if they lacked the authority.  Senator Marcos Daniel Pineda, who supported Camargo, was also accepted as impeded, while Richard Fuelantala of Aico was authorized to vote in favor of Camargo.  Senate President Lidio García expressed frustration with the CNE’s inconsistent actions, remarking, 'Me desconcierta que ayer dijeron una cosa y hoy otra. Deberían tener más claridad y seriedad, porque así ponen en riesgo las decisiones de esta mesa directiva. Y encima nos notifican en plena votación'.  The election underscores growing friction between President Gustavo Petro’s administration and the Constitutional Court, particularly over pension reform.

The party aims to secure about 25 senators—roughly a quarter of the chamber—by leveraging Uribe’s strong electoral base.  For instance, the Pacto Histórico won 2.3 million votes in 2022 and secured 20 seats, illustrating how vote totals translate into seats under the closed‑list system.  Uribe’s past electoral record is highlighted: in 2018 he topped the Senate list with 872,000 votes, the most ever, earning 19 seats for the party; in 2014 he helped the party win 20 Senate seats and 19 in the Chamber.  The article quotes party director Gabriel Vallejo saying, 'Si los temas judiciales se lo permiten, el presidente Álvaro Uribe será el número 25 en la lista al Senado (...) No es que él haya aceptado la nominación, él fue el que la propuso y obviamente para el partido es un honor que él esté pensando en un momento tan difícil para Colombia', and professor Yann Basset noting, 'Si Uribe es candidato evidentemente es una buena noticia para el Centro Democrático…'.  It also notes that Uribe was sentenced to 12 years of house arrest for witness bribery and procedural fraud on 1 August 2024, but lawyer César Augusto Vargas explains that he remains pres‑presumed innocent until a second‑instance verdict is issued, allowing him to continue participating in politics.  The piece presents these facts in a largely neutral tone, providing context and metrics without overt editorializing.

articles.title: Cristian Chazatar Elected New Representative of AICO - HSB Noticias
articles.summary: During the Extraordinary National Assembly of the Movimiento de Autoridades Indígenas de Colombia - AICO Por la Pacha Mama, engineer Cristian Chazatar was elected as the new legal representative of the organization. The assembly, convened in accordance with internal procedures and quorum requirements, included delegations from various territories across Colombia. It was presided over by Taita Germán Báez and organized by a temporary board with Taita Jackson Cuasapud as secretary. Chazatar was chosen by majority vote from 20 indigenous governors and governors with voting rights, recognized for his organizational experience and commitment to indigenous autonomy, self-governance, and political participation. After the election, he formally assumed his duties before the plenary. The event also featured a cultural segment led by Wayuu authorities, who performed traditional dances such as Yonna and ancestral chants, reinforcing intercultural dialogue and mutual respect. This process followed a failed convocation on September 13, 2024, in the Túquerres Indigenous Reserve, and allowed AICO to reaffirm its leadership structure, legitimacy, and territorial participation. The organization aims to consolidate a leadership that strengthens indigenous representation in political and community spaces, grounded in the recognition of the Right of the Peoples and their traditional customs and identities.
